To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the new bright flare observed in April 2007 by XMM- Newton is similar to the brightest flare ever observed from Sgr  A * in 2002, and that the three moderate flares that followed are similar to the other previously observed flares.

the new bright flare observed in 2007 has the same spectral characteristics as the very bright flare of October 3, 2002, and that the spectral characteristics of the three moderate flares of April 4, 2007, are compatible within the errors with those of the two bright flares.

(1) the brightest X-ray flare ever observed from Sgr A*, with a peak amplitude 100 times above the quiescent emission, has occurred on April 4, 2002 and (2) the new flare is very similar to the bright flare observed on October 3, 2002 by X-ray Multi-Mirror Mission-Newton (XMM-Newton).
In summary, our research is concerned with
a systematic investigation of the spectral properties of the X-rays flares from SGR A*.
the study of the X-ray variability of the Galactic center source Sgr A*.
a detailed analysis of X-ray flares and quiescent emission of the supermassive black-hole at the Galactic center.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Sgr A*'s flares are soft.
the X-ray spectra of all flares are similar.
the flaring spectra from Sgr  A * are softer than the non-flaring spectrum, although the difference in hardness is not very large.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the flares from SAG A* are characterized by the presence of an excess of column densities, which may be intrinsic to the emission region, and a soft spectrum with Γ = 2.

the X-ray flaring emission of Sgr A* can be described by a power law with an average photon index of 2.1 ± 0.1, and a column density of $9.8^{+0.8}_{-0.8} \times 1 0^{22}$  cm -2, taking into account dust scattering.
the X-ray spectra of the bright flaring events are similar to the quiescent X-ray spectrum of Sgr  A*, with the addition of excess absorption.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the X-ray flaring emission from Sgr A * has similar spectral properties, regardless of the peak luminosity.
the flares from SAG A* are not a single phenomenon, but a family of flares with a range of spectral properties.

the spectral properties of the flares are consistent with the scenario in which the X-ray emission is produced close to the black hole event horizon and is scattered by the hot dust in the vicinity of the central object.
